tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — TRACE THE LOW PATCH
tiles.details: Source-labelled Uvalde and Burnet field photographs show threadlike foliage and low patches. The 2023 Muhlenbergia revision reports upright culms about 7–30 cm, with older trailing stems sometimes reaching 1 m; earlier crew notes give 20–40 cm. Growth varies. Trace one flowering stem into the ground, but do not assert underground connections from overlapping shoots.
tiles.short: Low, very fine-leaved perennial; do not mistake a surface mat for proven rhizomes.
tiles.status: REAL FIELD HABIT — CONNECTED ROOTED BASE MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · EXPOSE THE UNDERGROUND GROWTH
tiles.details: M. utilis is a rhizomatous perennial. Carefully expose a single continuous underground stem with attached scales, nodes, roots and aboveground shoot where collection is permitted; replace disturbed soil. The archived grass-patch images show neither underground scales nor connected root system. A reclining shoot is not itself proof of a rhizome.
tiles.short: Confirm slender, SCALY rhizomes below soil; nimblewill instead roots at surface nodes.

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR AND ROLLED BLADE
tiles.details: The 2023 revision describes blades about 0.2–1.8 mm wide and a short truncate, decurrent membranous ligule 0.2–0.8 mm long. The CC0 close-up shows a pale sheath-junction region, NOT a measured free ligule. Photograph the attached blade–sheath junction front-on and in profile at 10–20× beside a 1-mm scale; a fresh blade cross-section should show truly involute margins. Do not label a sheath margin as the free ligule.
tiles.short: Very narrow, often inward-rolled blades; true membranous ligule 0.2–0.8 mm.
tiles.status: COLLAR SEARCH VIEW ONLY — TRUE LIGULE UNMEASURED

tiles.heading: 04 · FOLLOW THE ENTIRE NARROW PANICLE
tiles.details: The 2023 revision describes a 1–5 cm × 0.1–0.4 cm interrupted, contracted panicle with mostly appressed branches about 0.2–1.2 cm long. Existing CC0 head photograph demonstrates actual attached spikelets along a narrow rachis, not a ruler-calibrated branch series. Photograph the entire flowering axis emerging from the upper sheath and include a centimeter ruler.
tiles.short: Contracted, sometimes partly sheathed flowering head, about 1–5 cm long.
tiles.status: ATTACHED FLOWERING PHOTO — HEAD MEASUREMENTS FROM LITERATURE

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT A RIPE ONE-FLORET SPIKELET
tiles.details: According to Peterson and colleagues (2023), each spikelet has one fertile floret. The two subequal usually one-veined glumes are 0.5–1.4 mm (occasionally 2–3 veins); the lanceolate fertile lemma is 1.3–2.4 mm, unawned, and the palea about 1–2 mm. Remove the glumes in order, then expose the lemma, palea and floret with 1-mm scale under 10–20×. Current whole-spikelet photos cannot prove separate bract measurements or veins; never draw arrows to unseen structures.
tiles.short: Spikelet 1.4–2.4 mm; glumes 0.5–1.4 mm; lemma 1.3–2.4 mm, AWNLESS.

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + RELEASE GATE
tiles.details: Panel 8 is DIFFERENT-SPECIES M. schreberi for comparison only: its slender aboveground stolons can root at nodes, whereas M. utilis requires visible scaly underground rhizomes. Seep muhly (M. reverchonii) makes a tighter tuft and more open flowering panicle; pine muhly (M. dubia) is much larger, with a much longer ligule. Do not infer the held hybrid M. ×involuta from intermediate appearance. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: connected Texas underground scaly rhizome and rooted flowering culm; 1-mm calibrated true ligule and rolled blade section; dissected ripe glumes/lemma/palea; matched rooted nimblewill. NEEDS_SITE_QA: eight archived image records and eight panels, precise rights/creator/source, existing gross arrows and provisional captions, correct look-alike labels and mobile gallery. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until all decisive anatomy and public QA are verified.
tiles.short: Separate aboveground-rooting nimblewill from underground-rhizomatous aparejo.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Look for a VERY LOW rhizomatous muhly: numerous extremely fine, inward-rolled threadlike leaves, slender usually 20–40 cm culms and a short narrow flowering head, sometimes partly held inside the top leaf sheath. True creeping SCALY underground rhizomes distinguish it from surface-stolon nimblewill, but rhizomes must be exposed for confirmation.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: PHOTO 1 — WIDE fine grassy patch beside paving. Surface mat habit only, no buried stem demonstrated.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The 2023 revision describes blades about 0.2–1.8 mm wide and a short truncate, decurrent membranous ligule 0.2–0.8 mm long. The CC0 close-up shows a pale sheath-junction region, NOT a measured free ligule. Photograph the attached blade–sheath junction front-on and in profile at 10–20× beside a 1-mm scale; a fresh blade cross-section should show truly involute margins. Do not label a sheath margin as the free ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The 2023 revision describes a 1–5 cm × 0.1–0.4 cm interrupted, contracted panicle with mostly appressed branches about 0.2–1.2 cm long. Existing CC0 head photograph demonstrates actual attached spikelets along a narrow rachis, not a ruler-calibrated branch series. Photograph the entire flowering axis emerging from the upper sheath and include a centimeter ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: M. schreberi spreads by ABOVE-GROUND slender stolons which root at nodes, usually with short flattened leaf blades; M. utilis has underground scaly rhizomes and very fine involute blades. M. reverchonii forms a tight compact upright tuft with an open flowering panicle. Sporobolus may look similar but its spikelet structures differ on mature dissection.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: Look for a VERY LOW rhizomatous muhly: numerous extremely fine, inward-rolled threadlike leaves, slender usually 20–40 cm culms and a short narrow flowering head, sometimes partly held inside the top leaf sheath. True creeping SCALY underground rhizomes distinguish it from surface-stolon nimblewill, but rhizomes must be exposed for confirmation.
memory_rule: Aparejo grass: very FINE foliage + BELOW-GROUND scaly rhizomes — surface patch alone is not proof.
safety_note: Eight archived source-specific M. utilis photos, seven exact species gallery panels plus one labeled nimblewill different-species look-alike. A 317×251 collar-area image is not a calibrated short membranous ligule. Underground scaly rhizome and root connection still unphotographed. Preserve exact CC0/CC BY/CC BY-SA rights and scientific range holds.
field_rule: Use low fine-grass habit, actual narrow spikelet-bearing panicle, and narrow leaves to suspect aparejo; distinguish it from nimblewill by a positively seen scaly UNDERGROUND rhizome and true inner membranous ligule, not by inference from turf texture.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: M. schreberi spreads by ABOVE-GROUND slender stolons which root at nodes, usually with short flattened leaf blades; M. utilis has underground scaly rhizomes and very fine involute blades. M. reverchonii forms a tight compact upright tuft with an open flowering panicle. Sporobolus may look similar but its spikelet structures differ on mature dissection.
